title: GoHighLevel Forms Can Now Expire. Your Old Ones Still Cannot
desc: HighLevel added open and close dates to Forms, Surveys and Quizzes on August 27. The setting is off by default, so every form you already published stays open.
keywords: gohighlevel form scheduling, gohighlevel form expiry, highlevel forms surveys quizzes, gohighlevel lead capture, close a form automatically, gohighlevel agency workflow
cta: Want your HighLevel account audited before the next campaign runs?
body:
September 1, 2026. HighLevel has added scheduled open and close dates to Forms, Surveys and Quizzes, which means a registration page can finally stop accepting entries by itself. The detail that decides how much work this creates is buried in the August 27 changelog: existing forms, surveys and quizzes continue to work exactly as before when scheduling is not enabled. The setting is opt-in, so nothing you have already published is protected by it. Every campaign form you shipped before last week is still open, still collecting, and still firing workflows for an offer that ended.

What shipped

  1. A Schedule visibility setting now appears in Forms, Surveys and Quizzes.
  2. An opening rule set to either Right away or a specific date, so a page can be published in advance and go live on its own.
  3. A closing rule set to either Never or a specific date, after which new submissions are automatically blocked.
  4. A time zone field applied to both the opening and closing schedule.
  5. Two custom experiences, one shown before the window opens and one after it closes, each of which can be a designed page or a redirect to another URL.
  6. A preview of the unavailable page as visitors will see it.
  7. An off-by-default rollout. Anything already published keeps its previous behavior until someone opens it and turns scheduling on.

The real cost is not a bad visitor experience

The obvious framing is that a stale form embarrasses you, and it does. The expensive part happens after the submission. A form that never closes still creates a contact, still triggers the workflow attached to it, still appears in the lead report, and still puts a record in front of somebody whose job is to call it. Nobody logs that as waste, because it does not show up as a lost deal. It shows up as a slower response time on the leads that were real, a lower show rate on the calendar, and a lead count that looks healthier than the pipeline underneath it.

That distortion compounds in an agency account. Run twenty client sub-accounts with a few campaign forms each and the number of permanently open pages is measured in dozens, none of which anyone remembers building. The submissions arriving through them are indistinguishable in the CRM from leads that came from a live offer, which means the first person to notice is usually the client asking why their cost per booked call moved.

What it means for operators

Treat the backlog as the task, not the setting. Turning scheduling on for new builds takes a minute. The work is auditing what is already live. Sort published forms, surveys and quizzes by creation date, and flag anything tied to a dated thing: a webinar, an event, a cohort, a coupon, a contest, a seasonal promotion. Those are the ones still collecting.

Set the close date when you set the offer date. The close date is knowable at build time, because campaigns are planned before they are built. Filling it in then is the only version of this that survives contact with a busy month.

Redirect rather than dead-end. The expired experience can point at another URL, so late traffic has somewhere to go. A visitor who arrives two days after registration closed is a person with proven interest and bad timing, which makes them a waitlist signup or a next-cohort registration rather than a bounce.

Keep the window in one place. The schedule carries its own time zone field. Set it to the client's operating time zone rather than yours, or a deadline advertised as midnight will close at a time nobody announced.

This is the second HighLevel change in a week that hands agencies a control they previously had to fake with manual work, after workflow-level sender domains arrived on August 28. Both point the same way: campaign scoped settings instead of account wide ones. If you want your HighLevel build audited for the forms nobody remembers publishing, that is standard practice in our GoHighLevel work, and it is the first thing we check before running a lead generation campaign into an existing account.
faqs: What did HighLevel change on August 27, 2026?

HighLevel added a Schedule visibility setting to Forms, Surveys and Quizzes. It lets you choose when a page starts accepting submissions, when it stops, the time zone the schedule uses, and what visitors see before it opens and after it closes, either as a custom page or a redirect to another URL.
Does form scheduling apply to forms I already published?

No. The changelog states that existing forms, surveys and quizzes continue to work exactly as before when scheduling is not enabled. The setting is opt-in per asset, so anything already live keeps accepting submissions indefinitely until someone opens it and configures a closing date.
Why does a form that never closes cost anything?

Because the submission still runs. A late entry creates a contact, triggers the attached workflow and lands in the lead report even though the offer behind it has ended. The damage shows up indirectly as slower response times on genuine leads, lower show rates and a lead count that overstates real pipeline, rather than as an obvious loss.
What should visitors see after a form closes?

HighLevel lets you show a designed page or redirect to another URL. A redirect is usually better for campaign forms, because someone arriving after a deadline has demonstrated interest with bad timing. Sending them to a waitlist, the next cohort or a related live offer converts traffic that would otherwise bounce.
